copies.headline: WR Room So Deep It's Rude
copies.body:
Adam's actually done building rosters, he's just showing off now. Jaxon Smith-Njigba anchors a wide receiver corps that goes four deep before you hit a bad word — Chris Olave at pick 31 is theft, Rome Odunze gives him a legit WR3, and Jalen Coker in round 10 is pure lottery-ticket depth. Then round 7 happens and Jayden Daniels falls into his lap at +38 value, a sitting starting QB1 taken like a backup. Sam LaPorta anchors a shaky TE room that Mark Andrews (round 11, absurd value) quietly upgrades into respectable. The one soft spot is obvious: RB grades a D, with Kenneth Walker and Bucky Irving needing to stay upright and Rico Dowdle/Kenny Gainwell/Brian Robinson as the injury-report support group.
Efficiency plus ceiling is how you get a 228.1 roster score and a +50 value score in the same draft. This is what happens when the guy with the best career record in the league stops overpaying out of habit — 34-22 doesn't happen by accident, and neither does this.

copies.headline: Bijan and Lamar Bail Out a Thin Middle
copies.body:
Bijan Robinson at 1.02 is as safe a bell-cow anchor as this league offers, and Peter surrounded him with a receiver corps that should score in bunches — A.J. Brown, George Pickens, Tee Higgins is three legitimate X-receivers before you even get to Jalen McMillan filling in as the WR4. The real coup is Lamar Jackson falling to round 5, a 21-slot gift that turns the QB room from solid into a genuine advantage alongside a fallback in Dak Prescott taken way past his line. Tucker Kraft is a fine target-earner but the room behind him is empty, and this roster will punt the TE spot most weeks.
The RB room after Bijan is a mess of late-round dice rolls — Jonathon Brooks, Jordan Mason, Chris Rodriguez, Kyle Monangai — all bench-quality bets that only matter if injuries hit. Efficiency-wise Peter overpaid across the board to lock in this much talent, which tracks: he hasn't sniffed the title since going 13-1 in year one, and this looks like a man trying to buy his way back rather than out-scout the room.

copies.headline: Two Elite Tight Ends, One Actual Running Back
copies.body:
John's namesake pun aside, this team was built on a simple idea: dominate the two positions everyone else punts, then figure out the rest at the cabin. Bowers and McBride give him a two-headed TE room better than most starting WR corps, and pairing Puka Nacua at 1.04 with a McBride reach at 28 that still graded +9 value is the kind of quilt that wins championships in July. Kyren Williams at 45 was the steal of his draft, RB1 numbers at a round-4 price. Problem is after Kyren and a shaky Swift, the RB room is Corum, Tracy, and Keaton Mitchell — handcuffs pretending to be plans. Caleb Williams at QB7 with Stafford as insurance is fine, not a strength.
This is a top-heavy monster with real bye-week landmines at running back, but the ceiling is enormous. John's 10-4 in 2025 proved he can win with less; this roster gives him more. Still hunting that ring, still 3-6 against his brother.

copies.headline: Backfield Loaded, Wideouts an Afterthought
copies.body:
Noah built this thing from the ground up on running backs and dared the room to stop him. James Cook III at 1.8 and De'Von Achane at 2.17 is as good a one-two as anyone in the league drafted, and he kept stacking, adding Rhamondre Stevenson, Tyjae Spears, and a dirt-cheap Ray Davis as season-long insurance. Colston Loveland gives him a real TE1 target, and Drake Maye in round 5 is the kind of value that makes the room grumble under its breath. Garrett Wilson and Mike Evans anchor the receiving corps, but after that it's fog — Josh Downs was a full two rounds early, and names like Michael Wilson and Jordyn Tyson are lottery tickets, not plans.
The WR room is the whole ballgame here: if it holds even replacement level, this roster contends. Fitting, honestly, for a guy nobody drafts in round one either — the 2024 champ from the 7 seed knows how to win ugly.

copies.headline: Loaded Wide Receiver Room, Shaky Everywhere Else
copies.body:
CeeDee Lamb at 11 anchors this thing and the WR room backs it up nicely — DeVonta Smith gives you a legit WR2, Jameson Williams is the explosive TD-spike guy, and Khalil Shakir in round 11 is close to theft. Deebo at #107 is the one swing that missed; that room isn't hurting for volume, and Deebo's now a committee back playing receiver on a bad offense. RB is functional, not great: Chase Brown and Etienne split lead-back duties on your roster the way their own offenses split them in real life, Tuten and Aaron Jones round it out as flex depth with real bust equity if the top two stay healthy. George Kittle at pick 86 is the best value on the sheet, full stop — a top-5 TE at TE2 pricing.
QB is the crack in the foundation. Trevor Lawrence and Jordan Love is a room you're praying overperforms, not one that anchors a bye week. That's the Aura Farm pattern — always stacked somewhere, always exposed somewhere else, which is how you go 10-4 one year and 4-10 the next.

copies.headline: Logan Builds A Roster, Not A Curse-Breaker
copies.body:
Justin Jefferson at 10 and Saquon Barkley at 15 is about as clean a start as this league saw, and Logan kept pulling value after — Jeremiyah Love in Round 3 as a legitimate handcuff-to-lead-back bet, Tetairoa McMillan as a real WR2 in Carolina's offense, and Jalen Hurts falling to Round 6 is the single best value grab of the entire draft. Michael Pittman and Xavier Worthy add cheap volume, and Isaiah Likely was stolen a round late. The floor here is genuinely high.
The cracks: tight end is a wasteland behind Likely's injury risk, and the RB room outside Barkley and Love is Dobbins' knees and Tyler Allgeier's touches on a run-funnel offense. That's the profile of a team that wins the regular season and finds a new way to lose in January — which, given Logan's the reigning face of the #1 Seed Curse and the dress, tracks perfectly.

copies.headline: Backfield Loaded, Receivers an Afterthought
copies.body:
Leif built this thing from the ground up on the interior. McCaffrey at 5 and Henry at 20 gives him two true bell cows, and grabbing Montgomery in round 5 as the handcuff/flex insurance was smart, low-cost business. Then he doubled down at quarterback for reasons only he understands — Josh Allen at 29 is a legit steal, twelve slots below market, but circling back for Mahomes in round 13 as a QB2 is the kind of luxury pick that reads as either genius or a man who forgot he already solved the position. Pitts gives the TE room a pulse even if the room grades D+.
The receiver corps is where this falls apart. Adams and Diggs are both on the wrong side of 30, Marvin Harrison Jr. was a reach in round 7, and after that it's Jayden Reed and dart throws. Woody Marks 28 spots early and Kaelon Black 40 spots early torched real draft capital on bench depth. Loyal to the bit as ever, Joey Lunchbox built a monster and forgot it needs targets.

copies.headline: Gibbs Was the Easy Part
copies.body:
Mitchell took the top pick in the room and then spent the next fifteen rounds arguing with himself. Jahmyr Gibbs at 1.1 is correct and clean, and pairing him with Josh Jacobs gives the backfield real thump even if Jacobs at 25 overall cost nine picks more than the field was paying. Alvin Kamara falling to round 16 is the kind of found money that should offset a mess elsewhere, and it almost does — this RB room grades A and could carry the team by itself. The problem is everything hung around it. Nico Collins is a legit WR1, but DJ Moore, Courtland Sutton, Tank Dell and Jerry Jeudy is a receiving corps built entirely out of injury history and name recognition, not target share. Tyler Warren anchors a fine TE room, though Travis Kelce in round 10 was paying 2021 prices for 2026 snaps.
Jaxson Dart plus Daniel Jones at QB is a bet that neither will ever be the reason you win, which tracks — Mitchell's whole career is 7-7 seasons that somehow sneak into the bracket. This roster doesn't sneak anywhere without health.

copies.headline: All Gas, No Backfield
copies.body:
Isaac built a receiver room that would headline any other roster in this league and then seemingly forgot running backs exist. Chase, Nabers, McLaurin, Metcalf, Wan'Dale, Meyers — that's six capable targets, led by a true WR1 in Chase and a field-stretcher in Nabers who should combine for the most PPR points in the room by October. But the backfield is Javonte Williams as the RB2 overpay at pick 22, Cam Skattebo as the lone genuine value of the draft, and Jaylen Warren as your flex insurance policy nobody wants to need. Bo Nix forty picks early at QB and a TE room of Hockenson's health question marks and Kincaid's ceiling with no floor round out a draft that's basically one great position group carrying three shaky ones.
This is what happens when a guy still chasing his 11-3 start from 2022 falls in love with names in the mirror and forgets the mirror has other rooms in it. The receivers alone won't be enough — this team lives or dies on whether Skattebo becomes a real back by Week 6.

copies.headline: Backfield Hoarder Forgets Wide Receiver Exists
copies.body:
Jonathan Taylor at nine anchors this thing fine, and Quinshon Judkins in round three doubled down before CJ apparently remembered receivers exist. That's the whole draft in miniature: five different running backs on this roster — Taylor, Judkins, TreVeyon Henderson, Chuba Hubbard, Isiah Pacheco, Zach Charbonnet — stacked so deep that Henderson is basically a taxi-squad luxury item. Problem is the receiver room reads like an afterthought. Rashee Rice was already a reach at 16, Egbuka's solid but low-ceiling as a WR2, and after that it's Parker Washington and Alec Pierce hoping for touchdown variance. Joe Burrow in round six is the one shrewd move on the board, a QB1 arm at backup pricing, with Tyler Shough stashed behind him.
The bones are here — a workhorse back, a franchise QB found late — but starting Rice-Egbuka-Pierce most weeks caps the ceiling hard. CJ's brand is loaded defenses and empty banners; one winning season in four, and this roster's receiver corps isn't going to be the thing that changes that.

copies.headline: Four Wide Receivers, No Team Behind Them
copies.body:
Amon-Ra at 6 was fine, but the wheels came off almost immediately. Zay Flowers nine picks under market and Christian Watson nine under his own on top of that leaves Grant with a WR room that grades out well but was drafted like he forgot the other positions existed. Waddle and Godwin add to the pile-up of good-not-great pass catchers he'll be benching three of every Sunday, while Omarion Hampton is the lone bright spot at running back before the room disintegrates into Jadarian Price, Tony Pollard, JCM and Tank Bigsby — four committee pieces fighting over maybe one and a half startable roles. Kyler Murray and Baker Mayfield is a real QB roomz only in the sense that both players exist. Dallas Goedert in round 11 is a fine value, forty picks under market, but one good pick doesn't rescue a roster built on repeated runs at a position he already had.
Grant's whole deal is variance — 3-11, then 9-5, then 5-9 — and this roster is the visual representation of that chaos. Elite receiver corps, replacement-level everywhere else, QB by committee. Lord save him indeed.

copies.headline: The 12 Seed, Earned Honestly
copies.body:
Jeanty at 12 and Hall in round 3 is a fine RB foundation on paper, but everything built around it undercuts the plan. Drake London anchors the receiver room fine, but from there it's a parade of thin value: McConkey's a nice complementary piece, Carnell Tate and KC Concepcion are lottery tickets stacked on a team that needed sure things, and Jordan Addison at pick 84 was a full round early for a WR3 on a run-heavy offense. Herbert in round 8 is the one shrewd swing here, a genuine QB1 got at backup prices, but then Kaleb turned around and took Jared Goff too, because apparently one struggling bridge quarterback wasn't enough insurance. Fannin and Sadiq give you a TE room of theory, not production.
The efficiency score says he paid retail or worse almost everywhere else, and the roster grade agrees with the math. Three straight 8-6 finishes since the 2023 miracle run, and this draft reads like a team playing not to lose instead of trying to win — which, fittingly, is how you land in 12th.

intro: Three A's at the top and the draft still had a clean split down the middle — Adam, Peter, and John all walked out of the cabin with rosters that look finished, while the bottom five (Mitchell, Isaac, CJ, Grant, Kaleb) are already praying for a waiver-wire miracle by Week 4. Running backs went in bunches early and often, which is exactly why Noah's zoo of a roster and Logan's ground-and-pound build both grade out fine despite completely different strategies. Christian and Leif did the sensible middle-class thing and nobody will remember their teams until October. Grant and Kaleb's F's are the kind you frame and hang on the wall — a real achievement in the wrong direction.
